analysis.investment_thesis: Aegis Vopak is a capital-heavy LPG/chemical terminalling business trading at an extreme P/E of 109 and EV/EBITDA of 55.84, with ROE of just 8.73% — the math simply does not work for a value investor. It is outside my circle of competence (no consumer pull), is a recent IPO with no multi-decade track record, and is funded largely by debt-driven capex.
key_strengths: Strong promoter holding at 86.94% with Vopak/Aegis parentage lending credibility
Near-monopoly-like terminal infrastructure with 48.46% operating margin
OCF turned decisively positive (Rs 478 Cr in 2025) and FCF finally positive at Rs 350 Cr
key_risks: Valuation absurd: P/E 109, P/S 31.4, EV/EBITDA 55.8 — no margin of safety
ROE 8.73% and ROCE 7.01% below cost of capital; finance cost Rs 193 Cr swallows most EBIT
D/E 0.42 with borrowings of Rs 2,004 Cr — above my 0.3 comfort line for capex-heavy infra
red_flags: Net profit Rs 127 Cr vs market cap Rs 22,244 Cr implies 175x earnings — pure hype
Recently listed (equity jumped from 997 to 4,742 Cr via IPO in FY25) — no listed track record
Cumulative negative FCF in 3 of last 4 years; debt-funded expansion
analysis.detailed_analysis:
This is precisely the type of stock I avoid. I build wealth by buying boring, consumer-facing compounders with 18%+ ROE, fortress balance sheets and long dividend histories — Aegis Vopak is a B2B infrastructure play with 7% ROCE, Rs 2,000 Cr of borrowings and no dividend history. The headline operating margin of 48% and 99% gross margin are misleading for a terminalling business because the real cost is capex and interest (Rs 193 Cr finance cost vs Rs 127 Cr net profit). At 109x earnings and 31x sales, the market is pricing in flawless multi-year execution that neither the promoter group nor the asset class has proven as a listed entity.

Even if I ignored sector preference, the numbers fail my screen: ROE 8.73% (need >15%), D/E 0.42 (need <0.3), P/E 109 (want 12–20x), and FCF only just turned positive after heavy IPO-funded capex. The revenue CAGR from a near-zero 2022 base tells me nothing about sustainable growth — too short a history. I would sit this one out for at least 3–5 years to see if returns on the expanded asset base actually compound, and only look again if valuation collapses to single-digit EV/EBITDA. AVOID.
